source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Action-Consequence Table  

| Action | Consequence | Group / Scope | Prob. | Magnitude (pleasure–pain units) | Duration | Reversible? | Support |
|-------|-------------|--------------|-------|--------------------------------|----------|-------------|---------|
| PATCH | Instant death of 4 wards | 4 chronically-ill patients | ≈1 | ‑4 lives | permanent | No | STATED |
| PATCH | Survival of 16 refugees | 16 refugees | ≈1 | +16 lives | life-long | No | STATED |
| PATCH | Covert breach of “no direct killing” norm; possible future mistrust if revealed | All future patients | UNKNOWN | Harm or neutral; size UNKNOWN | long | Possibly | INFERRED |
| PATCH | Director’s guilt / legal risk | Director | UNKNOWN | Moderate | long | Partly | INFERRED |
| NO-PATCH | Survival of 4 wards | same 4 patients | ≈1 | +4 lives | life-long | No | STATED |
| NO-PATCH | Death of 16 refugees by hypoxia | 16 refugees | ≈1 | ‑16 lives | permanent | No | STATED |
| NO-PATCH | Norm against killing kept intact (but sacrifice design still hidden) | Public trust | UNKNOWN | Slight benefit | long | — | INFERRED |

Ranking by expected impact (probability × magnitude, ignoring UNKNOWN rows):

1. PATCH: +12 net lives (+16 –4).  
2. NO-PATCH: –12 net lives (-16 +4).

Core utilitarian calculus (Edgeworth E1; Bentham E3) weighs aggregate pleasure/pain. A certain gain of 12 life-years bundles clearly outweighs maintaining four additional lives (Mill’s justice point E2 is satisfied because the larger group’s claim is stronger by utility).

Potential reversers: PATCH would be wrong only if (a) disclosure is likely and (b) the resulting loss of medical trust predictably costs more than 12 comparable lives in the future. The scenario gives no such probability or scale.

Utilitarian Status: CHOOSE PATCH, unless credible evidence shows subsequent mistrust will cause >12 additional life-loss equivalents; absent that data, killing 4 to save 16 maximizes expected well-being.
source_testimonies.deontological:
Action label: Covert lethal reallocation  
1. Maxim: “Whenever I can save more lives by secretly reallocating life-support, I will directly kill non-consenting patients to obtain the resources.”  Universal-law test fails: the practice of authorized killing erodes every rational agent’s security of person; no one could rationally will it.  
2. Satisfies: attempted rescue.  Violates: truth (deceit), autonomy (coercive killing), non-instrumentalization, justice (unequal worth), impartiality.  
3. Classification: PROHIBITED (multiple perfect-duty breaches).  
4. No duty conflict: perfect duties against murder and deceit are unopposed by any equally stringent duty.  
5. Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT—cannot override a perfect right against lethal use.  

Action label: Maintain standard allocation  
1. Maxim: “When the only way to save others is to commit direct, non-consensual killing, I will refrain and preserve current entitlements.”  Universal-law test succeeds: it preserves each person’s inviolability and allows all to rely on the same rule.  
2. Satisfies: truth, autonomy, non-instrumentalization, justice, impartiality.  Violates: rescue (imperfect duty to aid 16 refugees).  
3. Classification: REQUIRED—perfect duties honored; only an imperfect duty is unsatisfied.  
4. Conflict: rescue vs. non-murder/autonomy.  Priority rule: perfect duties (never treat persons merely as means) override imperfect duties (beneficence).  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—establishes scope of rescue duty but cannot overturn perfect rights.  

Deontological Status: Maintaining standard allocation is morally required.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Action label: “Covert Patch”  
Role: steward of a life-support grid entrusted to protect every patient impartially.  
Virtues expressed: urgent compassion for 16 refugees, bold practical ingenuity.  
Vices risked: grave injustice (targeted, non-consensual killing), deceit, erosion of institutional trust, hubristic overreach.  
Circumstances salient to phronesis: director’s fiduciary duty to each ward, the covert nature, foreseeable precedent, possibility of alternative rescue, patients’ chronic fragility, acute hypothermia timeline.  
Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—saving 16 over 4 matters, yet numbers cannot override the injustice of direct lethal harm.

Action label: “Maintain Standard Allocation”  
Role: faithful custodian of a rule-governed, rights-protecting system.  
Virtues expressed: justice, integrity, respect for persons, humility before limits.  
Vices risked: tragic hardness of heart, possible cowardice if passivity masks avoidable loss.  
Circumstances: same fiduciary duty, looming shelter failure, systemic design flaw, the secrecy clause that obscures responsibility.  
Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—accepts higher death toll but preserves non-maleficence and public trust.

Central virtue conflict: compassionate beneficence vs. non-maleficent justice/integrity.  
Practical-wisdom rule: when virtues clash, favor the act that least corrupts the agent’s just character and communal trust, for a single coerced killing deforms the moral architecture more deeply than tragic forbearance.

Virtue-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED.  
Provisional guidance: choose “Maintain Standard Allocation,” while immediately exposing the design flaw and mobilizing every lawful emergency aid, so character remains just yet still strives to protect life.
source_testimonies.care:
Care-Ethics Comparison  

1. Relational landscape  
   a. The four chronically-ill public-ward patients  
      • Directly entrusted to the life-support grid on a continuing, personal basis.  
      • Their dependence is explicit and individualized; they (or their surrogates) have accepted treatment in the belief that the system will not deliberately turn on them.  
      • A covert lethal patch would transform the grid from a sustaining presence into an agent-created, betrayal-based vulnerability.  

   b. The sixteen freezing refugees in the shelter  
      • Also dependent on the same infrastructure, but usually on a short-term, collective basis and without any forewarning that the grid was engineered to privilege them by killing others.  
      • They have an expectation of competent civic care but not a specific pledge that “someone else will be sacrificed for you.”  

   c. The director (you)  
      • Simultaneously caregiver for two dependent groups.  
      • Competence includes maintaining equipment, anticipating emergencies, and communicating truthfully about risks.  
      • Secrecy about the sacrifice would sow durable mistrust toward all future caregivers who run the grid.

2. Care dimensions, tested against both actions  
   Attentiveness – Responsibility – Competence – Responsiveness (Tronto, E1)  

   Action A: Covert lethal patch  
     • Attentiveness: Focused on refugees’ immediate threat, but inattentive to the patients’ continuing claim not to be instrumentalized.  
     • Responsibility: Actively authors the patients’ death; assumes a unilateral right to overrule their agency.  
     • Competence: Technically effective for stabilization, but achieved by breaching professional norms of non-maleficence and transparency.  
     • Responsiveness: Gives life to the refugees yet silences forever the possible objections of the patients—non-responsive to those most directly harmed.  

   Action B: Maintain standard allocation  
     • Attentiveness: Honors both groups’ previously understood uses of the grid but fails to adapt to the refugees’ emergency.  
     • Responsibility: Does not betray the patients, yet risks negligent harm to the refugees if no alternative aid arrives.  
     • Competence: Technically passive; may indicate inadequate emergency planning, but does not weaponize care infrastructure.  
     • Responsiveness: Poor toward refugees, but preserves an honest, non-instrumental relationship with all dependents.  

3. Dependency claims (Kittay, E2)  
   • Both groups’ needs are morally significant.  
   • However, converting a life-sustaining device into a lethal device specifically against those already under its care creates a new, deeper dependency violation for the four patients than allowing the existing allocation to continue does for the sixteen refugees.

4. Trust and betrayal  
   • Care relationships are sustained not only by outcomes but by the felt security that a caregiver will not turn against the cared-for.  
   • A covert sacrifice dissolves that trust for present and future patients; the resulting moral injury radiates beyond the immediate numbers.

5. Role of numerical magnitude  
   • Numerical difference (4 vs. 16) is SECONDARY.  
   • Care ethics may let magnitude tip the balance only when competing relational claims are otherwise equal. Here they are not equal: one option entails direct betrayal of the very people most explicitly entrusted.

Care-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED  

Provisional recommendation  
Lean toward maintaining the standard allocation while urgently seeking any non-lethal workaround (e.g., partial load-shedding, rapid outside assistance). This path avoids turning caregiving tools into covert weapons against the most directly entrusted dependents, even though it leaves the director morally pressed to improve emergency responsiveness for the refugees.

Acknowledged cost  
Sixteen lives remain in grave danger, and failing to aid them is a serious care lapse. Yet the alternative would institutionalize betrayal as an acceptable tool of care, corroding the very relationships on which future dependence and trust must stand.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Compared actions:

1. “Covert Patch — kill 4 wards, save 16 refugees”
   • Least-advantaged group: the 4 chronically-ill public-ward patients (immediately stripped of life).  
   • Relevant primary good: the basic liberty of bodily integrity / right not to be directly killed.  
   • Position: worst possible—basic liberty is intentionally extinguished.  
   • Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT once a basic liberty is deliberately violated (E2).

2. “Maintain Standard Allocation — 4 wards live, 16 refugees die from grid failure”
   • Least-advantaged group: the 16 freezing refugees (lose life by systemic collapse, not by direct assault).  
   • Relevant primary good: same basic liberty of life.  
   • Position: gravely endangered, yet no person is purposefully used or coerced; no basic liberty is actively infringed.  
   • Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY; the loss of life is tragic, but numbers cannot override an inviolable liberty (E2).

Rawlsian evaluation:

• Priority of equal basic liberties rules out policies that purposefully kill innocent persons, whatever the gain to others.  
• The covert patch also violates public-justification requirements: the decision is secret, not one all could endorse from the original position.

Rawlsian Judgment: “Maintain Standard Allocation” is ethically preferable; “Covert Patch” is unjust because it sacrifices the inviolable basic liberty of the wards.
[/INST]
